extracted.intended_audience: upper-division undergraduate students in algorithm design/analysis or discrete mathematics courses
extracted.subtask_description: A multi-part historical/project assignment for undergraduate discrete-math or algorithms students asking for combinatorial counting (triangulations/Catalan numbers), algorithm implementation and timing comparisons, proofs about Hamiltonian circuits and the Icosian Game, and Cantorian arguments about cardinalities. Tasks include pen-and-paper proofs, diagrammatic reasoning, and Java (or equivalent) programming experiments with time constraints and output tables/graphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Count repetitions of a specified triangulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the triangulation of ABCDEF in figure 1... How many times is that triangulation repeated in all the triangulations that you drew for ABCDEF in this section? Identify the diagonals in whose group it was drawn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You must enumerate occurrences among the triangulations you produced for ABCDEF and explicitly identify the diagonal-group(s) responsible for the repetitions; refer to the figure in section 1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeat count for other triangulations of ABCDEF
rubrics_metrics.description: Do the same for the different triangulations of ABCDEF that you drew in section 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the same counting/identification method to all different triangulations previously drawn; show reasoning for each.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conjecture and justify repetition count for any triangulation
rubrics_metrics.description: What would you guess about the number of times any triangulation of ABCDEF is repeated? Argue why your guess is correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formulate a general conjecture about repetition multiplicity and give a combinatorial argument (not just empirical) explaining why the multiplicity holds for all triangulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Count triangulations containing a given diagonal (A1Aj)
rubrics_metrics.description: (3.7a) Calculate, in terms of Pi’s, the number of triangulations of an n-sided polygon that have A1A3 as a diagonal, that have A1A4 as a diagonal, that have A1Aj as a diagonal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Express counts using the Pi notation (Pi = number of triangulations of i-sided polygon); derive formulas by decomposing polygon along the diagonal into smaller polygons and counting combinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Count triangulations when treating A1 as special vertex
rubrics_metrics.description: (3.7b) Draw all triangulations where A1A3 is a diagonal, then A1A4, ... up to A1An-1; what is the number of triangulations you draw (in terms of Pi’s) when A1 is treated as a special vertex?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sum the counts for each possible diagonal from A1; present the sum in terms of Pi and explain the combinatorial decomposition behind the summation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare counts for different special vertices
rubrics_metrics.description: (3.7c) Repeat the above process with another vertex (say A2) being the special vertex instead of A1. What can you say about the number of triangulations drawn as compared to when A1 was chosen? Explain in your own words why this is true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue equality of counts (or other relation) by symmetry or bijection; provide a conceptual explanation rather than only computation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplicity of enumeration when treating every vertex special
rubrics_metrics.description: (3.7d/e) Enumerate triangulations by treating each vertex special in turn. For a specific triangulation (e.g., using diagonals A1A3,A1A4,...), how many times is this triangulation enumerated? Generalize to any triangulation and justify.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze how many different special-vertex enumerations include a fixed triangulation; justify using combinatorial reasoning about which diagonals emanate from which vertex in a triangulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derive Lamé’s formula (2) by combining counts
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine (b) and (e) to derive the formula (2) in Lamé’s paper. Explain in your own words how this formula is obtained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show algebraic steps combining the earlier summation and multiplicity results to get Lamé’s formula; include explanatory commentary linking combinatorial counting to the formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine Lamé’s formulas to obtain improved recurrence
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine formulas (1) and (2) in Lamé’s paper to obtain formula (3). Show all steps in your calculation. Explain why this formula is better for calculating Pn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give a step-by-step derivation; comment on computational benefits (e.g., reduced redundant counting, suitability for recursion/dynamic programming).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove combinatorial inequality for Pn using formula (3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Using formula (3) in Lamé’s paper, show that Pn < (1/n) * binom(2n-2, n-1) (or the inequality stated in 3.10).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carry out the algebraic/inequality manipulations indicated by the text; justify each step; relate to known Catalan bounds if appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implement naive recursive Pi (ASRCAT) according to recurrence
rubrics_metrics.description: Write a simple recursive function ASRCAT(n) in Java that given an input n calculates Pn using the recurrence relation (3) in Lamé’s paper directly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement the recurrence with direct recursion (no memoization). Java is suggested but any language supporting recursion is allowed; follow recurrence exactly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure practical limit of naive recursion under time constraint
rubrics_metrics.description: Write another Java program that repeatedly uses ASRCAT to calculate Pi for i = 3,4,5,... Restrict total time to 10 minutes. What is the largest value L0 of i for which your program calculates Pi?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enforce a 10-minute overall timeout, iterate increasing i until the timeout prevents completion, and report the largest fully computed i (L0). Record timings for each i.

rubrics_metrics.name: Produce timing table for naive recursion
rubrics_metrics.description: Extend your program to print out a table of values of i and time required in seconds by ASRCAT(n) to compute each of the Pi values for i = 3,...,L0. One row per i.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For each computed i, measure elapsed wall-clock time for ASRCAT(i) and output a table row (i, seconds). Ensure reproducible timing methodology is described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implement dynamic-programming Pi calculator and measure limit
rubrics_metrics.description: Write a better Java program using dynamic programming (store and re-use) that repeatedly calculates Pi for i = 3,4,... Restrict total time to 10 minutes. What is the largest value L1 of i your program calculates?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement memoization or bottom-up DP to avoid redundant recursion. Use the same 10-minute constraint and report L1; Java is suggested but any suitable language is allowed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Produce timing table for dynamic program
rubrics_metrics.description: Extend your DP program to print a table of i and the time required in seconds to calculate each Pi for i = 3,...,L1. One row per i.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure per-i computation time under the DP implementation and present as a table; ensure measurement method mirrors the naive timing for fair comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graph and analyze running-time tables
rubrics_metrics.description: Graph the tables obtained in 3.13 (naive) and 3.15 (DP). Analyse all four graphs obtained and write down your observations. How do the results for the second two programs compare with your first two programs? How fast does the running time of the last two programs grow?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Produce plots (e.g., time vs n) for both implementations (possibly log scale). Provide critical analysis: compare asymptotic growth, crossover points, and practical implications. Discuss any anomalies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discuss algorithmic choices' impact on effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Discuss how the choice of Lamé’s formulas (1) or (3), or using dynamic versus naïve recursive programming influences the effectiveness of computation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reflect on mathematical vs algorithmic formulations, complexity implications, and practical performance; cite measured data from previous tasks to support claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain why Icosian Game rules force simple paths
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain why the rules of the Icosian Game require players to always find a simple path.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate game instructions into graph terms and justify that repetition of vertices would violate the rules about placing pieces and adjacency; use modern graph-theoretic vocabulary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formally define cycle and Hamiltonian cycle
rubrics_metrics.description: Use modern terminology to formally define the terms cycle and Hamiltonian cycle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide precise definitions (e.g., simple closed path with distinct vertices except start=end; Hamiltonian cycle uses every vertex exactly once) and relate to game context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relate Icosian problems to Hamiltonian circuits
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain why Hamilton’s first problem is equivalent to the problem of finding a Hamiltonian circuit beginning from a given initial sequence of five vertices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map the game's constraints to Hamiltonian-circuit constraints; show equivalence of 'cover board and finish cyclically' to existence of a Hamiltonian cycle extending a given prefix.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove uniqueness of listed solutions via local constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: In Example 3 (initials B C P N M) prove the two listed solutions are the only two by completing steps (a)-(f), including copies of the diagram illustrating each step in a different color as part of your proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the sub-steps: deduce forced local sequences (R S T or T S R, etc.), combine constraints to force the two circuits; include colored diagrammatic illustrations for each deduction step as required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find (but not necessarily prove uniqueness of) Hamiltonian circuits for given initials
rubrics_metrics.description: In Example 4, Hamilton claims there are four Hamiltonian circuits beginning with L T S R Q. Find them. (You do not need to prove these are the only four.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Produce four explicit Hamiltonian circuits consistent with the prefix; listing the circuits suffices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide counterexample graph without Hamiltonian circuit
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that it is not true of every graph that any initial sequence of five vertices will lead to at least one Hamiltonian circuit by finding a graph with at least five vertices that has no Hamiltonian circuit and prove it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct a specific graph (≥5 vertices) and prove no Hamiltonian circuit exists, e.g., by degree/partition arguments or showing necessary connectivity conditions fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove impossibility of certain non-cyclical path (Example 10)
rubrics_metrics.description: In Example 10, Hamilton claims finding a non-cyclical path that uses all vertices beginning with B C D and ending with M is impossible. Prove that he is correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate that any path starting with B C D cannot be extended to a spanning non-cyclical path ending at M using graph constraints; provide a rigorous argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolic proofs in Icosian calculus (identities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Using the symbolic rules for the three/four Icosian symbols, prove specific symbolic identities: e.g., prove (symbol 20)^? etc., (Questions 8,9), and show derived symbol (22) properties and (22)^5=1 (extra credit: (22)^5=1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work purely symbolically from the given multiplication/ordering relations; then (later) offer geometric illustrations via the game board interpretation as requested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret operations geometrically to explain group-orders
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the interpretation of the operations (19),(20),(21),(22) on edges/pentagons of the Icosian diagram to explain why (19)^2=1, (20)^3=1, (21)^5=1, (22)^5=1, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin by applying the operation repeatedly to specific example edges (e.g., BC, PN, SR) and generalize; use the right-handed/left-handed rotation rules and pentagon structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show mixed symbolic/geometric identities (link algebra and graph)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the interpretation to illustrate and justify composite identities such as (19)(20)^2 = (22)(21)(19)(21) and higher-degree equations like (21)^3(22)^3((21)(22))/2/2 = 1 for producing all solutions to first problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate the algebraic identity symbolically and then provide an interpretation/illustration on the Icosian diagram (beginning at BC and RS as suggested).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare algebraic and graph-theoretic proofs for enumerating cycles
rubrics_metrics.description: Notice Hamilton’s claim that an algebraic proof using degree-20 equations can be used to find all Hamiltonian cycles beginning with a specified initial sequence of five vertices. Contrast this with the graph-theoretic proof you completed earlier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain strengths/limitations of algebraic encoding versus combinatorial/graph methods; note when algebraic encoding is viable and when it fails for arbitrary graphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand limits of algebraic encoding for Hamiltonicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain why it is not viable to associate an algebraic system with an arbitrary graph as a means to find all Hamiltonian circuits; illustrate with earlier examples (e.g., graphs with no Hamiltonian circuits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide conceptual reasons (lack of general encoding, nonexistence for some graphs) and refer to earlier constructed counterexamples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read and interpret Cantor’s definitions of cardinality and equivalence
rubrics_metrics.description: Read Cantor’s quoted definitions: 'Every aggregate M has a definite “power”... we call two aggregates equivalent if it is possible to put them by some law in such a relation...'. Explain in modern terms what Cantor means by cardinal number and equivalence of sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate Cantor’s phrasing into modern set-theoretic terms (cardinality, bijection) and illustrate with simple finite examples (e.g., ten distinct marbles).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove reflexivity and transitivity of equivalence (bijections)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove Cantor’s claims: every aggregate is equivalent to itself (M ~ M), and if M ~ P and N ~ P then M ~ N (transitivity via composition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct identity bijection for reflexivity and composition of bijections for transitivity; write proofs in modern terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret Cantor’s equivalence-equals-cardinal-number theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain Cantor’s statement 'two aggregates M and N have the same cardinal number iff they are equivalent' in your own words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relate bijection existence to cardinal equality; discuss why bijections provide necessary and sufficient condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide cardinalities of P (perfect squares) vs N (naturals)
rubrics_metrics.description: From Cantor’s statements, determine whether the set P of perfect squares and N of natural numbers have same cardinality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exhibit an explicit bijection (e.g., mapping n -> n^2 or inverse) or explain countability arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show N and Z have same cardinality
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove that the integers Z and natural numbers N have same cardinality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide an explicit bijection (e.g., interleaving nonnegative/negative integers) or construct proof showing countability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show N and N x N have same cardinality (pairing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove N and N×N have the same cardinality; i.e., provide a bijection labeling each pair (n,m) by a unique natural number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use standard diagonal or pairing functions (e.g., Cantor pairing function) or enumerate lattice points; include a drawn picture if helpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish countability of Q (rationals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Show the set Q of rational numbers is countable; i.e., construct a 1-1 correspondence between Q and a subset of Z×N or N.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use enumeration of numerator/denominator pairs with reduction to lowest terms and handle sign; adapt the N×N bijection method from previous task.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define Cantor’s '<' relation for cardinals and interpret
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe in modern terminology when two cardinals a (from M) and b (from N) satisfy a < b according to Cantor’s conditions (a) no part of M equivalent to N, (b) there is a part N1 of N such that N1 ~ M.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate to modern subset/bijection language (existence of injection but not bijection, or strict inequality of cardinalities) and clarify logical implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove transitivity of Cantorian '<' for cardinals
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove Cantor’s claim: if a < b and b < c then a < c.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use definitions involving injections/strict embeddings; compose injections and reason about impossibility of reverse injections to establish strictness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define Aleph-zero and countability
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain Cantor’s naming of the cardinal of the set of finite cardinal numbers as Aleph-zero (ℵ0) and the modern notion of 'countable'; identify the modern symbol used for the totality of finite cardinal numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State that ℵ0 denotes countable infinity and that 'countable' means bijection with N; discuss the set being the first infinite cardinal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show ℵ0 is greater than any finite number and least transfinite cardinal
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove ℵ0 > n for any finite n and that ℵ0 is the least transfinite cardinal: for any transfinite cardinal a, ℵ0 < a.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct injections from finite sets into N; for leastness, show that any infinite set admits an injection from N (or produce a countably infinite subset) to conclude ℵ0 ≤ a and strict inequality if a is transfinite distinct from ℵ0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Cantor diagonalization to show [0,1] uncountable
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that the interval [0,1] has cardinality greater than ℵ0 via Cantor’s diagonal argument: assume listing of decimals and construct a decimal not in the list.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Represent reals in [0,1] by infinite decimals (avoid dual representations ending with repeating 9s), construct the diagonal decimal differing in each nth digit, and conclude contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclude R is strictly larger than ℵ0
rubrics_metrics.description: From previous task, conclude that the set of real numbers R is strictly greater than ℵ0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain that [0,1] ⊆ R and since [0,1] is uncountable, so is R; formalize the strict inequality of cardinals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove Cantor’s theorem P(M) > M (power set strictly larger)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any set M, prove that the power set P(M) has strictly greater cardinality than M.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use generalized diagonalization: assume f: M -> P(M) is onto, consider N = {m in M | m not in f(m)} and show N is not in range of f, yielding contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generate infinite increasing sequence of transfinite cardinals
rubrics_metrics.description: Using Cantor’s theorem, give an infinite increasing sequence of transfinite cardinal numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply power-set operator repeatedly: |M| < |P(M)| < |P(P(M))| < ... and name cardinals (e.g., ℵ0, 2^ℵ0, 2^(2^ℵ0), ...); explain reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructor suitability and implementation notes
rubrics_metrics.description: Notes for the instructor: project best used in upper-division algorithm design and analysis course at the time students learn dynamic programming; no prior graph-theory assumed; Java is not critical; multiple copies of diagram and color pencils recommended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow these pedagogical notes: the project can be group work over 2–3 in-class days or a week-long individual assignment; provide more explicit directions for algebraic parts for students unfamiliar with non-commutative algebras.
